hook.text: A 2013 study found 78% of Americans admit to regifting. Only 5% said they'd never been offended by receiving one.

buildup.text: In Western cultures, regifting implies you didn't value the original gift enough to keep it.

discovery.text: But in many Pacific Island cultures, regifting is expected. Gifts are meant to circulate, not accumulate.

twist.text: The Kula ring is essentially a vast regifting network. Value comes from the chain of owners, not the object.

climax.text: Sustainability advocates now promote regifting as environmentally responsible rather than socially awkward.

punchline.text: Regifting is either rude or wise—depending on your culture.

quiz.question: What percentage of Americans admit to regifting?

details.summary: Regifting — passing along a received gift to someone else — is taboo in many cultures yet increasingly accepted in others. In Japan, regifting is deeply insulting. In the US, it is becoming normalized as practical and sustainable.
details.whyItMatters: The regifting debate reveals competing values: efficiency versus thoughtfulness, sustainability versus social obligation. How a culture views regifting exposes its deeper priorities about gift exchange.
takeaways: Regifting is deeply insulting in Japanese and many Asian cultures
Over 50% of Americans admit to regifting
Sustainability advocates promote regifting as anti-waste practice

faq.question: Why is regifting considered rude?
faq.answer: Regifting implies the original gift was not thoughtful or valued enough to keep. It suggests the recipient did not care about the giver's effort and intent.

faq.question: When is regifting acceptable?
faq.answer: Most etiquette experts agree regifting is acceptable when: the item is unused and in original packaging, it genuinely suits the new recipient, there is no risk of the original giver discovering it, and you are not regifting out of laziness but thoughtfulness.
